screens.title: Advanced DR with AWS Resilience Hub and DR Drills
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you’ll learn how to move disaster recovery from paper into practiced capability. We start with AWS Resilience Hub, a centralized way to define resilience policies, discover application components, and get actionable recommendations that map to RTO and RPO targets. Then we’ll walk through how to plan, execute, and analyze DR drills so your team can validate recovery steps and assign corrective work. Finally, we’ll introduce AWS Fault Injection Simulator so you can inject controlled failures and observe whether auto scaling, load balancers, and failover behave as expected. As you listen, imagine a pilot-light analytics app with a four-hour RTO and one-hour RPO. We will use that scenario to show how assessments reveal gaps, how a drill exercises those gaps, and how a targeted FIS experiment safely validates parts of your recovery flow. A common misconception is that a single test proves resilience; instead, resilience improves through repeated, measured drills and post-mortems. By the end you’ll know how to define policies, run safe experiments, and turn lessons into automation and documentation updates.

As you practice, aim to make tests repeatable and to update documentation after every drill.

screens.title: What is AWS Resilience Hub?
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Resilience Hub is a centralized service that helps you define resilience policies, discover the resources that compose an application, and assess that application against measurable targets like RTO and RPO. In practical terms, Resilience Hub imports your CloudFormation stacks, Resource Groups, or AppRegistry applications and builds a model of what actually runs your application. It then compares that model against predefined or custom policies to give you a resilience score and a list of prioritized recommendations. For example, if a database lacks cross‑region backups the assessment will flag this as an RPO risk and recommend cross‑region automated backups or read replicas. A common misconception is that Resilience Hub replaces architectural review. It does not; it augments review by providing automated, data-driven findings that reduce manual blind spots. Use Resilience Hub reports to drive your drill scope: prioritize tests against the highest‑risk items and track remediation progress over time. How would you use these findings to select your next drill target? What is AWS Resilience Hub? means resilience hub centrally models and measures application resilience, mapping resources to rto/rpo policies and producing actionable recommendations.. In practical terms, a centralized service to define, assess, and track application resilience. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept

What is AWS Resilience Hub?

Resilience Hub models applications, checks compliance with RTO/RPO policies, and returns a resilience score plus targeted recommendations.

• Discovers resources via CloudFormation stacks, Resource Groups, or AppRegistry.
• Compares architecture to resilience policies to find single points of failure.
• Produces recommendations like cross-region backups, auto scaling, or replication.
Key Takeaway

Use Resilience Hub to convert resilience goals into prioritized fixes and measurable improvement over time.

Assessment Snapshot
Resilience Score
67
Score based on policy compliance and resource risks.
Top Recommendation
Enable cross-region automated backups for RDS to meet tight RPO targets.
Discovery
Detected resources: EC2, RDS, S3. Source: CloudFormation stack import.
Why it matters
Automated assessment focuses drill efforts on the highest-risk components first.
Common mistake
Treating Resilience Hub findings as complete proof. Always validate recommendations with drills and restores.

screens.title: Defining Resilience Policies: RTO and RPO
screens.narratorSegment: Resilience policies are the concrete expression of business tolerance for downtime and data loss. RTO, the recovery time objective, defines the maximum acceptable time to restore functionality. RPO, the recovery point objective, defines the maximum acceptable data loss window. When you create a resilience policy in Resilience Hub you map each application to an RTO and RPO target; assessments then measure compliance. A concrete example: an analytics dashboard with an RTO of four hours and an RPO of one hour requires database backups or replication that preserve at most one hour of data loss and runbooks that restore operations within four hours. A common misconception is that low RTO/RPO targets only demand faster hardware. In reality, meeting tight targets often requires architectural changes—cross-region backups, read replicas, automation for promotion, and tested runbooks. Use policy-driven findings to prioritize which architecture changes to automate and which to validate in the next drill. How would you choose between point-in-time backups and near real-time replication for your RPO? Defining Resilience Policies: RTO and RPO means rto and rpo convert business tolerance into specific engineering requirements that guide assessments, recommendations, and drills.. In practical terms, turn business tolerance into measurable recovery targets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition

Resilience Policies: RTO & RPO

Translate business needs into recoverability targets and let assessments report compliance.

RTO
Maximum acceptable downtime; measured in time to restore functionality.
RPO
Maximum acceptable data loss; measured in time since last recoverable snapshot or replica.
Example
Pilot-light analytics app with RTO 4 hours and RPO 1 hour: requires automated backup or replication and tested promotion steps to meet targets.
Decision guidance
  • Point-in-time backups are acceptable for higher RPO windows and simpler restores.
  • Near real-time replication suits low RPOs but increases complexity and testing needs.
  • Always validate chosen approach with a restore test during a drill to ensure it meets the policy.
Misconception check
Tighter RTO/RPO is not solved by faster hardware alone; it often requires automation, replication, and runbook readiness.

screens.title: Discovering Applications and Resource Mapping
screens.narratorSegment: Discovery is the first step to an automated resilience assessment. Resilience Hub can import application definitions from CloudFormation stacks, AWS Resource Groups, or AppRegistry entries and then map underlying resources—EC2 instances, RDS databases, S3 buckets—into a single application model. This mapping matters because assessments must know which resources support critical paths and where single points of failure exist. In practice, you register an application, point Resilience Hub at the CloudFormation stack or Resource Group, and it will scan the resources and build the model for assessment. A concrete example: importing a CloudFormation stack representing your e-commerce stack will reveal whether RDS lacks cross-region backups or whether an Auto Scaling Group has insufficient subnets for multi-AZ resilience. A common mistake is assuming discovery is perfect; always validate the discovered model and add missing resources before relying on the score. After discovery, schedule an assessment and use the produced report to pick the first drill target. content.html:
Process Flow

Discovery & Resource Mapping

Import CloudFormation, Resource Groups, or AppRegistry to build an application model for assessment.

  1. Register app: point Resilience Hub at the CloudFormation stack or AppRegistry entry.
  2. Scan resources: Resilience Hub enumerates EC2, RDS, S3, and other components.
  3. Validate model: confirm all critical resources are included before assessment.
Example
Importing a CloudFormation stack for an app should reveal the RDS instance that requires cross-region backups and the ASG that needs multi-AZ subnets.
Discovery Checklist
  • Confirm CloudFormation stacks are current and include all resources.
  • Check tags and identifiers to ensure correct grouping into one application model.
  • After import, review the detected resource list before running the assessment.
Why validate?
Missing resources produce falsely optimistic resilience scores. Manual confirmation keeps assessments honest.
Pro tip
Use consistent tagging and keep CloudFormation templates current so discovery reflects reality.

screens.title: Assessing Resilience and Interpreting Recommendations
screens.narratorSegment: Assessment produces a resilience score and a set of recommendations that point to specific architectural or configuration gaps. Interpreting these outputs requires context: a low score for a database often indicates RPO risk, while a low score for compute might indicate single points of failure or insufficient subnets. Recommendations range from enabling cross‑region backups to configuring Auto Scaling Groups or adding multi‑AZ replication. When you evaluate recommendations, consider impact, complexity, and how they change your ability to meet RTO/RPO. For example, enabling cross‑region automated backups addresses RPO by ensuring recent backups exist in another region, but the recommendation only becomes reliable after you test restoring from that backup in a drill. A typical mistake is implementing recommendations without planning the verification step. Prioritize fixes that close the largest gap relative to your policy, then schedule drills to validate them. What single recommendation would you prioritize for a four‑hour RTO and why? Assessing Resilience and Interpreting Recommendations means use scores to prioritize remediation by impact on policy targets and then verify changes with focused drills and restores.. In practical terms, how to read scores and prioritize fixes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Comparison

Interpreting Scores & Recommendations

Not all recommendations are equal—prioritize by policy impact, testability, and implementation cost.

Database risk
Often affects RPO; cross-region backups or replication are typical fixes.
Compute risk
May indicate single AZ dependencies or ASG misconfiguration affecting RTO.
Key Takeaway
Implement the highest-impact, testable recommendations first, then verify with a drill that includes restores.
Prioritization checklist
  • Which recommendation reduces the largest gap to your RTO/RPO?
  • Can the change be tested in a drill or restore within a reasonable window?
  • Does the fix require additional automation or IAM changes to be effective?
Verification
A recommendation is only trusted after you run a drill or perform a restore test that demonstrates the desired RTO/RPO.
Pitfall
Treating recommendations as finished work without scheduling verification leads to false confidence.

keyIdea.title: Action
keyIdea.text: Use the Resilience Hub create-app CLI to import CloudFormation stacks and begin automated assessment, then validate discovery and set policies.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Create an app from a CloudFormation stack

Example CLI to register an application so Resilience Hub can discover resources.

# Example: Register an application defined by a CloudFormation stack
aws resiliencehub create-app \
    --name "MyWebApp" \
    --description "E-commerce web application" \
    --resource-mappings '[{"ResourceType":"CfnStack","LogicalResourceId":{"Identifier":"MyWebAppStack"}}]'
Checklist after create-app
  • Confirm the discovered resource list contains your EC2, RDS, and S3 resources.
  • Select or create a resilience policy with your RTO/RPO targets.
  • Run an assessment and download the report for drill planning.
Practical note
Substitute your stack identifier. If discovery misses resources, add them manually before trusting the assessment.
Misconception
Creating the app does not set RTO/RPO; you must select or author a resilience policy separately.

screens.title: Planning a DR Drill
screens.narratorSegment: Effective DR drills begin long before you run commands. The planning phase defines scope, objectives, participants, success criteria, and rollback plans. Start by choosing the application and a realistic disaster scenario, for example a full regional outage of the primary region. Define precise objectives such as verifying a four-hour RTO and one-hour RPO, and identify which recovery steps need validation—promotion of a read replica, AMI-based EC2 launches, or DNS failover. List required participants: operations, DBAs, developers, and business stakeholders as observers. Create a communication plan that tells stakeholders when they’ll be informed and how updates will be provided. Critically, draft a rollback plan that allows you to revert if the drill causes unexpected issues; safety is why many teams simulate failures rather than actually making production unhealthy. Finally, document success criteria in measurable terms: application endpoints respond within X seconds, reports are accessible, and data is current within the RPO. Which part of planning do you think most organizations rush, and why? keyIdea.text: Drill planning requires scope, measurable objectives, a clear communication plan, and a robust rollback strategy to make tests safe and useful.

content.html:
Process Flow

Planning a DR Drill

A good plan makes execution safe and the results actionable.

• Define scope: which app and what failure mode.
• Set objectives: RTO and RPO targets to validate.
• Identify participants: ops, DBAs, app owners, business stakeholders.
• Establish communication and rollback procedures.
• Set success criteria with measurable checkpoints.
Example: Pilot Light Drill
Scope: Internal analytics app. Objectives: RTO 4 hours, RPO 1 hour. Participants: DevOps, DBAs, App owners. Rollback: revert DNS and terminate DR resources if rollback needed.
Why planning matters
Detailed planning avoids ambiguity during execution, keeps stakeholders informed, and reduces risk of accidental production impact.

Execution

Executing a DR Drill

Run controlled simulations, follow the runbook, and capture detailed logs to measure recovery performance.

  • Pre-checks: AMIs, templates, read replica synchronization, runbook availability.
  • Simulate failure: stop instances, fail Route 53 health checks, or run FIS in staging.
  • Execute recovery: promote DB, launch EC2 in DR region, update DNS, verify app.
  • Document timestamps to compute RTO and check data for RPO.
Verification checklist
Endpoint accessibility, report generation, data integrity checks, RTO time measurement, and confirm no undocumented manual steps were needed.
Common mistake
Skipping detailed time logs prevents root cause analysis and makes it hard to validate you met RTO/RPO.

screens.title: Introduction to AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS)
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Fault Injection Simulator is a managed service for running chaos experiments that inject faults into AWS resources so you can observe system behavior and validate recovery mechanisms. FIS supports actions such as stopping or terminating EC2 instances, rebooting databases, injecting network latency, or creating C P U stress. The goal is to test whether your automation—Auto Scaling Groups, load balancers, and failover scripts—responds correctly under controlled fault conditions. A concrete example is terminating a small percentage of EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling Group to verify that the ASG launches replacements and the load balancer maintains healthy targets. Safety is paramount: start experiments in non-production, use stop conditions to guard against escalating impact, and grant the FIS IAM role only the minimal permissions required. Core Tool

AWS Fault Injection Simulator

Run controlled chaos experiments to validate Auto Scaling, load balancing, and failover automation.

keyIdea.title: Template
keyIdea.text: FIS templates declare targets, actions, and stop conditions; use filters to narrow scope and always include safety controls.

content.html:
Code Example

FIS Experiment Template

Template to terminate two random EC2 instances tagged as production in us-west-2; used to validate ASG and ALB behaviors.

{
  "description": "Terminate random EC2 instances in primary region",
  "targets": {
    "Instances": {
      "resourceType": "aws:ec2:instance",
      "selectionMode": "COUNT(2)",
      "parameters": {
        "filters": [
          {"path": "State.Name", "values": ["running"]},
          {"path": "Tags.Environment", "values": ["production"]},
          {"path": "Tags.Region", "values": ["us-west-2"]}
        ]
      }
    }
  },
  "actions": {
    "TerminateInstances": {
      "actionId": "aws:ec2:terminate-instances",
      "parameters": {
        "instanceIds": "${Instances}"
      }
    }
  },
  "stopConditions": [
    {"source": "none"}
  ],
  "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:role/FISActionsRole"
}
What to verify
ASG launches replacement instances, ALB healthy host count returns to acceptable levels, and application remains functional.
Safety checklist
Run in staging first; set stop conditions tied to application health; limit IAM role permissions to necessary actions only.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Continuous Testing Cadence
screens.narratorSegment: A recurring mistake is treating DR testing as a one-off event rather than an ongoing program. Resilience is a journey: architectures change, people rotate roles, and services are updated, so quarterly or semi-annual drills keep your procedures current. Another common pitfall is excluding business stakeholders from planning and post-mortem reviews; they ensure recovery priorities align with business impact and can help define realistic success criteria. Safety misconfigurations in FIS experiments—overly broad IAM roles, missing stop conditions, or running high-impact experiments in production without staged testing—are avoidable by following a staged approach. Start in staging, do low-impact failures, validate metrics and alarms, then increase intensity as confidence grows. Automate what you can: AMI copy, template validation, and scripted DNS failover reduce manual delays in recovery. Finally, track resilience score improvements in Resilience Hub after each remediation to measure progress objectively. Which cadence makes sense for your application and why? Best Practice

Common Mistakes & Cadence

Avoid single tests, include business stakeholders, and stage experiments to build confidence safely.

  • Run drills regularly—quarterly or semi-annual—to capture architectural drift and personnel changes.
  • Involve business stakeholders to align objectives and success criteria with operational impact.
  • Stage FIS experiments: staging → low-impact production → higher-impact tests.
Automation opportunities
Automate AMI copying, CloudFormation validation, and scripted DNS updates to shorten recovery steps and reduce manual error.
Key takeaway
Make testing repeatable, measurable, and progressively challenging so resilience strengthens over time.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you’ll learn how to move disaster recovery from paper into practiced capability. We start with AWS Resilience Hub, a centralized way to define resilience policies, discover application components, and get actionable recommendations that map to RTO and RPO targets. Then we’ll walk through how to plan, execute, and analyze DR drills so your team can validate recovery steps and assign corrective work. Finally, we’ll introduce AWS Fault Injection Simulator so you can inject controlled failures and observe whether auto scaling, load balancers, and failover behave as expected. As you listen, imagine a pilot-light analytics app with a four-hour RTO and one-hour RPO. We will use that scenario to show how assessments reveal gaps, how a drill exercises those gaps, and how a targeted FIS experiment safely validates parts of your recovery flow. A common misconception is that a single test proves resilience; instead, resilience improves through repeated, measured drills and post-mortems. By the end you’ll know how to define policies, run safe experiments, and turn lessons into automation and documentation updates.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to use AWS Resilience Hub to define resilience policies that map to RTO and RPO targets, discover application components automatically, and interpret resilience assessments. You will also plan and run structured DR drills that include pre-defined scope, participants, success criteria, and rollback plans, and you will perform post-mortem analysis to capture learnings and assign corrective actions. Additionally, you will design safe AWS Fault Injection Simulator experiments that test Auto Scaling Groups, load balancers, and database failover, while respecting stop conditions and minimal IAM permissions. Each objective pairs practical skills with why they matter: policies give measurable targets, drills validate your runbooks, and FIS helps you prove automation behaves under stress. A common misconception is that tools alone ensure resilience; instead, combining assessment, drills, and experiments produces reliable improvement. As you practice, aim to make tests repeatable and to update documentation after every drill.

These objectives translate into concrete operational capabilities. First, using Resilience Hub you will be able to set and enforce RTO and RPO policies so tests have measurable targets. Second, you will design drill procedures that include communication and rollback plans to keep stakeholders safe and informed. Third, you will compose FIS experiment templates that target specific resources and include safety stop conditions, ensuring tests reveal system behavior without causing uncontrolled outages. Finally, you’ll run post-mortems that generate assignable action items and update documentation. A common misconception is that resilience is only an engineering task; in truth, it spans operations, application owners, and business stakeholders. When teams internalize these practices, DR moves from a checklist into a habit: repeatable tests, reliable automation, and documented improvements. Skills and Outcomes means translate assessments into measurable drills and safe experiments, then close the loop with a post-mortem-driven improvement process.. In practical terms, how these skills map to operational practices. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

AWS Resilience Hub is a centralized service that helps you define resilience policies, discover the resources that compose an application, and assess that application against measurable targets like RTO and RPO. In practical terms, Resilience Hub imports your CloudFormation stacks, Resource Groups, or AppRegistry applications and builds a model of what actually runs your application. It then compares that model against predefined or custom policies to give you a resilience score and a list of prioritized recommendations. For example, if a database lacks cross‑region backups the assessment will flag this as an RPO risk and recommend cross‑region automated backups or read replicas. A common misconception is that Resilience Hub replaces architectural review. It does not; it augments review by providing automated, data-driven findings that reduce manual blind spots. Use Resilience Hub reports to drive your drill scope: prioritize tests against the highest‑risk items and track remediation progress over time. How would you use these findings to select your next drill target? What is AWS Resilience Hub? means resilience hub centrally models and measures application resilience, mapping resources to rto/rpo policies and producing actionable recommendations.. In practical terms, a centralized service to define, assess, and track application resilience. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Resilience policies are the concrete expression of business tolerance for downtime and data loss. RTO, the recovery time objective, defines the maximum acceptable time to restore functionality. RPO, the recovery point objective, defines the maximum acceptable data loss window. When you create a resilience policy in Resilience Hub you map each application to an RTO and RPO target; assessments then measure compliance. A concrete example: an analytics dashboard with an RTO of four hours and an RPO of one hour requires database backups or replication that preserve at most one hour of data loss and runbooks that restore operations within four hours. A common misconception is that low RTO/RPO targets only demand faster hardware. In reality, meeting tight targets often requires architectural changes—cross-region backups, read replicas, automation for promotion, and tested runbooks. Use policy-driven findings to prioritize which architecture changes to automate and which to validate in the next drill. How would you choose between point-in-time backups and near real-time replication for your RPO? Defining Resilience Policies: RTO and RPO means rto and rpo convert business tolerance into specific engineering requirements that guide assessments, recommendations, and drills.. In practical terms, turn business tolerance into measurable recovery targets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Discovery is the first step to an automated resilience assessment. Resilience Hub can import application definitions from CloudFormation stacks, AWS Resource Groups, or AppRegistry entries and then map underlying resources—EC2 instances, RDS databases, S3 buckets—into a single application model. This mapping matters because assessments must know which resources support critical paths and where single points of failure exist. In practice, you register an application, point Resilience Hub at the CloudFormation stack or Resource Group, and it will scan the resources and build the model for assessment.
